stances.claim: On July 19 at the Philippine Embassy in The Hague, the government honored three outstanding Filipino jurists for their exemplary membership in UN-recognized international tribunals: the late CJ Cesar Bengzon (ICJ), former Inquirer publisher Raul C. Pangalangan (ICC), and the late Senior Associate Justice Florentino P. Feliciano (WTO Appellate Body).

Justice Toy Feliciano was a world-class scholar and jurist -- UP BA summa cum laude, UP LLB magna cum laude, Yale LLM and JSD; taught at UP, Yale, and The Hague Academy of International Law; SyCip Salazar managing partner before joining the SC in 1986 -- and from CJ's 1995 SC entry, served as the senior associate justice and Third Division chair whose intellect made colleagues 'careful not to pick an intellectual duel with him.'

Feliciano was sympathetic and patient with CJ as a 1995 Court neophyte without prior judicial experience -- having himself been a neophyte without judicial background -- and this generosity is part of what made him a model jurist.

Feliciano retired early to accept election as a member, later chair, of the WTO Appellate Body -- an honor he alone holds in the country; though CJ believes Feliciano merited an ICJ seat, the ABW suited his commercial-and-international-law expertise. American colleague James Bacchus called him 'The Aristotelian' for his mastery of reason and logic as 'the torch of wisdom and discoverer of truth.'

Feliciano's Aristotelian zeal in the ABW reflected his SC zeal -- to open colleagues' eyes to 'pure logic and unadulterated reason' deciding cases fairly and objectively, 'almost stoically, with only the Constitution, laws, and precedents as guides and masters.'

Yale's Reisman placed Feliciano 'in the great tradition of Holmes, Cardozo, and others' -- and because Reisman is known to be conservative with language and timid with praises, the claim should not be mistaken as braggadocio. CJ's own law-dean and 'lifelong guru' Jovito R. Salonga (Harvard LLM, Yale JSD) called Feliciano 'one of the finest alumni of Yale' among all students including Americans.

Had Feliciano stayed on the SC, he could have been chief justice; but he chose international tribunal service where his expertise in commercial and international law was put to more productive use -- hence CJ's epithet: 'The Global Aristotelian Jurist.'

notable_anecdotes: The Philippine National Group composition disclosure -- Reynato S. Puno, Jose C. Vitug, Raul Pangalangan, and 'yours truly as PNG chair' -- quietly revealing CJ's continuing institutional role decades after retirement, and the PNG's role in nominating ICJ Judge Iwasawa Yuji.

Feliciano's biographical CV stacked as a single paragraph -- UP summa, UP LLB magna, Yale LLM, Yale JSD, taught UP/Yale/Hague Academy, SyCip Salazar managing partner -- making the credentialing itself the argument.

The 'careful not to pick an intellectual duel with him' memoir from CJ's Third Division chairmanship under Feliciano -- one of the most candid CJ admissions of being intellectually outmatched by a senior justice.
James Bacchus's 'The Aristotelian' nickname -- preserved as the column's titular framing, with Bacchus quoted directly that Feliciano 'was (their) great teacher.'

Reisman's Holmes-and-Cardozo placement -- paired with CJ's defensive note that 'Reisman is not known to exaggerate; quite the contrary, he is reputed to be conservative with his language and timid with his praises' -- modeling how to authenticate hyperbolic praise.

Salonga's verdict -- 'Toy is one of the finest alumni of Yale not just among Filipinos but amongst all students including Americans' -- quoted with CJ's parenthetical that Salonga himself was a Harvard LLM and Yale JSD, making the praise itself doubly authoritative.

The counterfactual close -- 'Had he stayed on the Court, he could have been chief justice but he chose to spend his remaining years of intellectual statesmanship in an international tribunal' -- turning Feliciano's departure into evidence of stature rather than loss.
CJ's own coined epithet -- 'The Global Aristotelian Jurist' -- extending Bacchus's nickname with the 'Global' modifier to capture Feliciano's international dimension.

one_paragraph_summary: On July 19 at the Philippine Embassy in The Hague, the government honored three outstanding Filipino jurists for their exemplary membership in UN-recognized international tribunals: the late CJ Cesar Bengzon (ICJ), former Inquirer publisher Raul C. Pangalangan (ICC), and the late Senior Associate Justice Florentino P. Feliciano (WTO Appellate Body). Keynote speakers were ICJ Vice President Kirill Gevorgian, CJ Alexander G. Gesmundo, and ICJ Judge Iwasawa Yuji (nominated by the Philippine National Group at the Permanent Court of Arbitration, comprising retired CJ Reynato Puno, Justice Jose Vitug, Judge Pangalangan, and CJ as PNG chair, exercising the UN-Charter-granted PCA right to nominate ICJ judges). The Supreme Court additionally published a collection of Feliciano's decisions and resolutions, and CJ was given the honor of writing the Foreword (six times the column's length) -- summarized here. Justice 'Toy' Feliciano was a world-class scholar and jurist: UP BA summa cum laude, UP LLB magna cum laude, Yale LLM and JSD; taught at UP, Yale, and The Hague Academy of International Law; SyCip Salazar managing partner before joining the SC in 1986. When CJ entered the Court in 1995 as 'a Court neophyte in every sense of the word,' Feliciano was already senior associate justice and Third Division chair -- 'our source of enlightenment for difficult issues of law' -- but sympathetic and patient with neophyte colleagues. He retired early to accept membership and chairmanship of the WTO Appellate Body, an honor 'he alone holds in our country.' American colleague James Bacchus called him 'The Aristotelian' for his mastery of reason and logic 'as the torch of wisdom and discoverer of truth,' and described him as 'their great teacher.' Yale's W. Michael Reisman placed him 'in the great tradition of Holmes, Cardozo, and others' -- and because Reisman is 'reputed to be conservative with his language and timid with his praises,' the claim is no braggadocio. CJ's own 'lifelong guru' Dr. Jovito R. Salonga (Harvard LLM, Yale JSD) called him 'one of the finest alumni of Yale not just among Filipinos but amongst all students including Americans.' Had he stayed on the Court, he could have been chief justice -- but he chose the WTO Appellate Body for his remaining 'years of intellectual statesmanship.' Hence CJ's coined epithet: 'The Global Aristotelian Jurist.'
